notes.meaning: A Canaanite king living in the southern desert heard Israel was approaching and launched an attack, capturing some Israelites. God allowed this initial defeat to test His people and teach them not to rely on their own strength. It reminded the nation that victory in the Promised Land would come only through God's help.

Israel responded to their loss by making a solemn promise to the Lord. They asked for His help and promised to completely destroy the Canaanite cities, giving everything over to God rather than keeping any plunder for themselves. Turning to God in prayer during difficult times shows genuine trust in His deliverance.

God heard Israel's prayer and gave them victory over the Canaanite army. The Israelites fulfilled their vow and named the area Hormah, which means complete destruction. This triumph reversed an embarrassing defeat their parents had suffered in the very same place almost forty years earlier.

Because the king of Edom refused to let Israel cross his land, the people had to travel south toward the Red Sea to detour around Edom. The journey was hot, rough, and took them farther away from the land they wanted to enter. Deep weariness set in, and the people grew impatient and frustrated along the way.

The people openly complained against both God and Moses, asking why they were brought out of Egypt just to die in the desert. They claimed they had neither bread nor water and spoke with disgust about the manna God gave them daily. Their discontent blinded them to the miraculous care God had provided all along.

God punished the people's rebellion by sending venomous snakes throughout the camp. These snakes were called fiery because their bites caused severe burning pain, intense fever, and death for many Israelites. God showed the people that the desert was full of danger and that they were entirely dependent on His protection.

The people recognized their wrongdoing, came to Moses, and admitted they had sinned by speaking against the Lord and against him. They begged Moses to pray that God would take the snakes away. Moses showed great love and patience by immediately praying for the very people who had insulted him.

God told Moses to shape a model of a poisonous serpent and place it high on a pole. Instead of removing the snakes right away, God provided a way of escape so that anyone who looked at the bronze figure would live. God often chooses simple or unexpected ways to heal, requiring people to trust His word alone.

Moses made a snake out of bronze and lifted it up on a pole for all to see. Whenever someone was bitten, they simply looked at the bronze snake in faith and were healed. Jesus later explained that just as this snake was lifted up, He too would be lifted up on the cross so that everyone who believes in Him will have eternal life.

After the plague of serpents was resolved, the Israelites packed up camp and moved forward to Oboth. This site lay along the eastern border of Edom as they worked their way around that kingdom. Each new camp brought them one step closer to the Promised Land.

Moving forward from Oboth, the Israelites camped at Iye-abarim in the wilderness on the eastern side of Moab. They obeyed God's command not to invade or bother the Moabites, who were distant relatives descended from Abraham's nephew Lot. Israel stayed outside their borders and pressed steadily north.

Leaving Iye-abarim, the people journeyed north and set up camp by the Valley of Zered, a stream flowing west toward the Dead Sea. Crossing this valley marked a major milestone in their history. By this point, the older generation that had refused to enter Canaan forty years earlier had completely passed away.

Israel next moved on and camped along the Arnon River, a deep ravine that marked the border between Moab and the Amorites. Because the Amorites had previously captured this land north of the river from Moab, Israel could travel here without violating God's command to respect Moab's borders. They were now directly on the edge of Amorite territory.

These verses quote from an ancient historical collection called the Book of the Wars of the Lord, which recorded famous battles and victories. The passage describes the ravines of the Arnon River and the slopes reaching toward the city of Ar in Moab. Quoting this well-known poem proved that the land north of the Arnon had passed into Amorite hands, giving Israel a lawful right to march there.

The Israelites traveled next to Beer, a name that means well. At this spot, the Lord told Moses to gather the people together so that He could give them water. Unlike earlier times when water was provided after bitter complaining, here God graciously promised water before anyone even grumbled.

In joyful gratitude, the Israelites sang a song calling for the water to bubble up from the dry ground. The leaders and nobles helped by using their staffs to open the sand under Moses' direction. This joyful response showed a refreshed spirit in the nation, pairing willing human effort with God's miraculous provision.

The Israelites continued marching through several stopping places, moving from Mattanah to Nahaliel, then to Bamoth, and finally to a valley near the top of Mount Pisgah. Pisgah overlooked the desert wasteland and provided a view near the plains of Moab. This brought Israel directly opposite the Jordan River, looking toward the land God had promised them.

Israel sent messengers to King Sihon of the Amorites, asking for permission to pass peacefully through his kingdom. They promised to stay strictly on the main highway, leaving his fields, vineyards, and private wells untouched. This fair and peaceful request showed that Israel sought peace first and did not desire unnecessary war.

King Sihon refused Israel's request and chose not just to defend his borders, but to march his entire army out into the wilderness to attack Israel at Jahaz. His stubborn pride and hostility left him without any excuse. By attacking Israel without cause, Sihon brought swift judgment and destruction upon his own kingdom.

Israel defeated Sihon in battle and took possession of his entire country between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers. They did not push past the Jabbok into the land of Ammon, both because Ammon's border was fortified and because God had ordered Israel not to touch Ammonite territory. God gave His people a complete victory while keeping them faithful to His commands.

The Israelites captured all the Amorite towns and settled in them, including the capital city of Heshbon and all its surrounding villages. Taking these cities gave the people a secure base east of the Jordan River. It also gave them practical experience in victory before crossing into the main land of Canaan.

This explains that Heshbon was the royal city of King Sihon, who had previously defeated a former king of Moab and taken all the territory down to the Arnon River. This background is important because it shows that Israel did not take land that belonged to Moab. They conquered land that belonged to the Amorites by right of recent war.

Ancient poets had composed a song celebrating Sihon's original victory over Moab, inviting people to come and see the rebuilt city of Heshbon. The poem described Sihon's army as a sweeping fire that burst out of Heshbon and burned down Moabite strongholds along the Arnon. Quoting this song proved that Sihon had completely conquered this region before Israel ever arrived.

The poem proclaimed doom upon Moab and mocked their pagan god Chemosh for being utterly unable to rescue his people. Chemosh could not stop his worshippers from being killed, turned into refugees, or carried away as captives by Sihon. The passage highlights the complete uselessness of false gods when real danger arrives.

The final lines of the song celebrate how Israel turned the tables on the proud Amorites and overthrew them completely. The cities that Sihon had taken from Moab, running from Heshbon down to Dibon and Medeba, were now captured and ruined by Israel. Those who had conquered others through violence ended up losing everything to the people of God.

Having defeated Sihon, the Israelites set up camp and lived in the conquered territory of the Amorites east of the Jordan. This fertile region provided space and pasture for the nation and their large herds of livestock. It foreshadowed the final rest and home that God had long promised to Abraham's descendants.

Moses sent scouts to explore Jazer, a fortified Amorite town north of Heshbon, and Israel captured both the town and its surrounding villages. They drove out the remaining Amorites to make the region safe for their families and herds. Careful preparation and swift obedience allowed them to clear out remaining pockets of enemy resistance.

Israel next turned north along the road leading to Bashan, a fertile region famous for rich pastureland and strong oak trees. Og, the king of Bashan, gathered his entire army and marched out to confront Israel at the town of Edrei. Like Sihon, Og chose war instead of seeking peaceful terms.

The Lord spoke directly to Moses and commanded him not to fear King Og, promising that the king, his people, and his land were already handed over to Israel. God assured Moses that the battle would end just as victoriously as the fight against Sihon. God's promises give courage and peace even when facing powerful and intimidating enemies.

Israel defeated Og in battle, striking down the king, his sons, and his whole army until no survivors remained, and then they took possession of his land. This victory completed the conquest of the lands east of the Jordan, later given to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. It proved to the new generation that the Lord was fully capable of conquering every giant and taking the Promised Land.
